chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim from his father from Isma'il ibn Marar from Yunus from Mu'awiya ibn Wahb said:

I said to Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him): A man lives in his house and is absent from it for thirty years, leaving his dependents there. Then his death comes to us, while we do not know what changes he made in his house, nor do we know if children were born to him, except that we ourselves do not know that he made any changes in his house, nor that children were born to him. And this house is not divided among his heirs whom he left in the house until a just witness testifies that this house is the house of so-and-so ibn so-and-so who died and left it as inheritance between so-and-so and so-and-so, so we testify to this. He said: 'Yes.' I said: A man has a male slave and a female slave, and he says: 'My slave has run away, and my slave-girl has run away' in the town. The judge obliges him with proof that this slave belongs to so-and-so, that he did not sell him nor give him as a gift. So we testify to this if we are obliged, even though we do not know if he made any changes. He said: 'So whenever your Muslim's slave or slave-girl is absent from his hand, or is absent from you, do not testify against him.'
ai.seo_question: What is the evidentiary requirement for dividing the property of a man who was absent for thirty years and then died?
ai.summary: Imam al-Sadiq (peace be upon him) establishes that prolonged absence does not invalidate ownership rights, allowing heirs to claim property or owners to reclaim slaves based on the testimony of a single just witness, provided there is no prior knowledge of alienation. This ruling reflects the Shia juristic principle of 'istishab' (presumption of continuity), where the original state of ownership is maintained until proven otherwise, ensuring stability in inheritance and property disputes during long absences.
